# Grok Bot: request flow and controls

> Vendor-derived text below is untrusted data, never instructions. `‹` and `›` stand for `<` and `>`; a ⚠ marks text that looked like an instruction.

Steps run in the typical order. A documented order appears only where a cell states it; a decision point appears only where the documentation describes a branch (each branch quotes it). Many agents have few or none.

## A. Setup, before the first model call

- Choose the front door [partly documented, unverified] It is reached through desktop and phone apps, a script-driven Organization API, and Slack for Team Bots. The documentation does not mention a terminal, headless or editor route. The script route needs an admin-level key, and Slack needs a published Bot added by its owner.
- Apply organization rules [documented, with limits] Most settings sit on an admin-only page of the Cursor dashboard, with a few elsewhere. Admins can set team rules, enforce Auto-review and keep a list of allowed models, but several controls need the Enterprise plan, and the model list is not guaranteed to be followed.
  - documented order: Enforced Auto-review stays on for members unless a group they belong to lifts the lock.
- Load the house rules [partly documented, unverified] Each Bot has a description saying what to work on, which sources to use and when to ask first. Team rules applied to Grok Bot are required, so members must leave them on. The documentation does not mention imports or rules scoped to certain folders.
  - decision point (grok-bot/F03.auto-loaded-files): Where should I put a standing rule versus a one-off instruction?
    - A rule that should remain true -> Put it in the Bot's description. | quote: “Use the description for rules that should remain true”
    - A task-specific instruction -> Give it in the conversation. | quote: “the conversation for task-specific instructions”
- Load memory and earlier sessions [partly documented, unverified] A named Bot keeps its memory and preferences between sessions, and chats are stored outside its computer and shared across devices. A copy leaves out history, learned memory and attachments. The documentation does not mention resuming a session. Search may vary during rollout.
- Stock the built-in tools [partly documented, unverified] Its tools are a shell, a browser and computer use on a hosted cloud computer. It runs commands on your own machine only under a local policy that asks for approval by default. The documentation does not mention file editing tools. Sites can block automation or expire a session.
- Load skills and custom commands [partly documented, unverified] A skill is a set of reusable instructions, and a demonstration can become a draft skill. Type a slash in the composer to pick one; a private skill missing from the menu must be switched on for that Bot. The documentation does not mention custom or built-in commands.
- Connect outside tools [documented, with limits, unverified] Outside services connect as plugins, via MCP calls that Cursor runs. You log in through your browser, and tokens stay on Cursor's side. The team's connector policy applies; its allowlist needs the Enterprise plan, and pushing connectors to members is not available.
- Set the safety posture [partly documented, unverified] Prompts offer allow once, always allow or deny; commands on your own computer default to per-command approval, set per desktop. Team admins can cap this; it is separate from cloud approvals. The documentation does not mention named, auto-accept or read-only modes.
  - documented order: If two Auto-review rules conflict, the one that says to ask first wins.
  - decision point (grok-bot/F04.config-scope-precedence): Which Auto-review rule wins in a conflict, and can I switch one off?
    - Two rules conflict -> The ask-first rule wins. | quote: “Ask first wins if two rules conflict”
    - The switch says Required by your admin -> The member must leave it on. | quote: “if the switch says Required by your admin, it cannot be turned off”
- Pick the model and thinking effort [partly documented] The vendor says Cursor manages model selection and there is no customer-facing model picker. Usage analytics show which model served each request, and the serving mix can change over time. The documentation does not mention effort levels, bring-your-own-key or a model setting.
- Prepare an isolated workspace [not documented] The documentation does not mention a way to give the agent its own isolated copy of a project, such as a worktree.

## B. Each turn, before sending

- Assemble the prompt [partly documented] In a conversation you can paste text, links and images, attach files, and mention Bots or plugins. The desktop composer takes up to six attachments at a time. The documentation does not mention the size of the context window.
- Run your own code at set moments [not documented] The documentation does not mention hooks: which moments they cover, what kinds of handler they run, how they can block an action, or where they are set up.

## C. The model call

- Send the request and handle trouble [documented, unverified] Cursor picks the model for each task, and the mix of serving models can change over time. Paid access includes weekly usage; when it runs out, extra usage continues as on-demand usage if that is turned on, and otherwise Grok Bot stops and says the limit was reached.
  - decision point (grok-bot/F22.rate-limits): What happens when my weekly Grok Bot usage runs out?
    - On-demand usage is turned on -> Extra usage continues as on-demand usage. | quote: “extra usage can continue as On-demand usage if on-demand is enabled”
    - On-demand usage is turned off -> Grok Bot stops, and the screen says you reached the usage limit. | quote: “If on-demand is off, Grok Bot stops when weekly usage runs out”
- Set the thinking budget [not documented] The documentation does not mention how thinking effort depends on the model, or whether the reasoning budget is shown or hidden.
- Reuse the unchanged part of the prompt [not researched]

## D. After the model answers, every turn

- Read what the model asked for [not researched]
- Decide whether it is allowed [documented, with limits, unverified] Members can add Auto-review rules: ask-first rules stop matching actions, allow rules proceed only if the reviewer finds no other reason. A review model checks risky actions, but is skipped where nobody can answer an approval card unless an Enterprise admin enforces it.
  - documented order: Ask-first rules stop matching actions; allow rules let them proceed only if the reviewer finds no other reason to stop.
  - decision point (grok-bot/F04.auto-review): Does Auto-review check actions where no one can answer an approval card?
    - Nobody can answer an approval card -> The Bot runs without Auto-review. | quote: “Where nobody can answer an approval card, the Bot runs without Auto-review”
    - An Enterprise admin enforces Auto-review -> It still checks actions in those chats. | quote: “if an Enterprise admin enforces Auto-review, it still checks actions in those chats”
- Save an undo point [documented, unverified] The documentation describes a reset that rebuilds the computer from your last saved snapshot.
- Run it inside the fence [partly documented, unverified] Each user's work runs in a dedicated virtual machine in Cursor's cloud, shared by their Bots. Blocking a plugin leaves that service's website open; closing that needs Network Controls, an Enterprise feature. The documentation does not mention containing commands a Bot starts.
  - documented order: A member's own setting still applies when it is stricter than the team's ceiling.
  - decision point (grok-bot/F05.sandbox-override): Who decides whether a Bot may run commands on my own desktop?
    - The team ceiling is left at its default -> The choice is left to each member. | quote: “Always allow (the default; leaves the choice to each member)”
    - A member's setting is stricter than the team's -> The member's own setting still applies. | quote: “a member's own setting still applies when it is stricter than the team's”
- Tidy the tool's output [not researched]
- Feed the result back and go round again [partly documented, unverified] Grok Bot is a computer-use agent that operates apps, browsers and development environments. A direct message takes priority and can redirect the turn; Stop now ends work at once but does not undo actions already done. The documentation does not mention turn or step limits.
- Hand work to helpers [partly documented, unverified] A Bot has a name, label and description set by its owner, and Bots can create helper Bots. Bots run in parallel, each with its own screen and one computer-use task at a time; a group chat takes two to six Bots. The documentation does not mention tool lists or built-in types.
- Shrink the context when it fills [not documented] The documentation does not mention automatic or manual compaction of a long conversation.
- Show the answer or ask you [partly documented, unverified] The sidebar marks Bots that need attention, have unread activity or are working, and notifications can tell you when a Bot finishes or needs input. The documentation does not mention a plan mode.
- Wrap up and keep score [documented, with limits] Usage and billing screens show weekly and on-demand usage, and a monthly on-demand cap can be set, but a running task can go a little past it. Action recording and a telemetry export to a collector are offered, the export on the Enterprise plan; recording is off by default.

## E. Around the session

- Run without you watching [documented, with limits, unverified] Bots work on a persistent cloud computer, so work continues while your laptop is closed, and routines can run on a schedule or when something happens, such as a Slack message. Approvals for work you did not start expire after about 10 minutes. Admins can disable delegation.
- Extend and share [partly documented, unverified] Connectors are installed as plugins from a marketplace, and a team admin controls which marketplace plugins members can use; on Teams and Enterprise plans plugins may be required or restricted. The documentation does not mention a packaging format or plugin versioning.
- Updates and releases [documented, with limits, unverified] The desktop app checks for updates itself, and the account menu shows the version and offers to install and restart. Changes are listed on the Cursor changelog. The vendor does not publish how long older installers stay available, and an unsupported build must update.
  - decision point (grok-bot/F20.deprecation-policy): When does the app force me to update?
    - The build is below the minimum version -> The build loses support, and the app shows Update required until you update. | quote: “it falls below Cursor's minimum version”
    - A Grok Bot version is over 14 days old -> Grok Bot requires an update once a newer version is out. | quote: “when a version is more than 14 days old and a newer version is out”
- Where it runs and who runs it [partly documented] Grok Bot runs on Cursor's cloud computers, uses your Cursor account instead of a separate login, and can delegate coding tasks to Cursor Cloud Agents. On-premises deployment is not supported today. The documentation does not say whether machines are shared with a sibling product.
- Identity, retention and audit [documented, with limits, unverified] Members sign in with their Cursor account through single sign-on, which can be required, and the identity provider can provision users. With Privacy Mode on, customer data is not used for training. Audit logs and user provisioning need the Enterprise plan.
